<reason>Both sides argued cleanly and respected the format, but B built and sustained the more analytically rigorous case. B's causal-identification critique of conditional prediction markets (a policy's conditional price cannot cleanly separate the policy's effect from the conditions that triggered the policy) was never actually resolved by A — A's "narrower conditioning" answer in Rebuttal 2 only makes the confound more granular without removing it, and B correctly flagged this in the next speech. B also successfully complicated A's "auditability beats lobbying" claim by noting that visible trades don't reveal purpose, and exposed a real tension in A's own case: the "documentation forces disagreement to be explained" mechanism A relies on is a governance rule, not an inherent property of markets, meaning A's mechanism collapses into needing the very institutional enforcement A criticizes as toothless. B's closing crystallized this decisively ("Money moves a price; it does not force an official to revise a forecast or choose a better policy"), landing the last, unanswered blow on A's central rhetorical claim that "money moving a price cannot be ignored." A's closing was punchy but mostly reasserted its asymmetry claim rather than repairing the exposed gap. A had strong framing, good use of plausible corporate/forecasting examples, and a clever turn accusing B's reform list of secretly describing a market, but B directly rebutted that by distinguishing accountability requirements from subsidized trading, and that distinction held up through the rest of the debate.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2/Closing combination — pointing out that narrowing conditional contracts doesn't resolve the causal-identification confound, and then closing with "money moves a price; it does not force an official to revise a forecast" — most damaged A's live route to victory by showing the market signal's disciplinary force depends on the same institutional enforcement A was trying to bypass.</best_rebuttal>
